summary:
Nizhny Novgorod Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender transition is banned, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no discrimination protection is available to LGBT+ people. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records these as country-wide conditions applying to this oblast.

That note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, but that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, as are people in the North Caucasus. For a trans visitor the trans-specific finding is the operative one: identity as such, not only public advocacy, places a person in the category the note expects to meet the persecution threshold.

Enforcement is live and documented. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, of which 98 were administrative and three criminal. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison.

Three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years' imprisonment. Charges at that level attach to printed and displayed material, which means a trans visitor's own visible expression, documents or publications can attract the same machinery as the identity itself.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office note treats the North Caucasus as a distinct and more acute risk area within Russia, where people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution regardless of the lower general assessment for LGB people elsewhere. Nizhny Novgorod Oblast is not named in that regional finding, and no separate regional assessment is recorded for it.

The extremism designation has produced convictions in both the administrative and criminal tracks, so the same conduct can be processed as a minor offence or as a felony depending on repetition and circumstances. The three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 illustrate the upper end, facing up to 12 years, while repeated display of banned symbols alone carries up to four years.

Human Rights Watch's reporting of at least 20 criminal charges opened from January 2024 onward indicates that the criminal track is expanding rather than settling into a small number of test cases.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nizhny Novgorod Oblast have no legal route to change gender markers on official documents, since legal gender transition was banned nationally in 2023, and no access to gender-affirming care through lawful channels for the same reason.

No anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, services or education, and same-sex partnerships confer no legal recognition, including for inheritance, hospital access or next-of-kin status.

The UK Home Office note records that 139 people across Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, a figure covering the national population rather than this oblast alone.

Residents face the same extremism exposure as visitors: 101 convictions had been issued by June 2025, 98 administrative and three criminal, and repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison.
outOfScopeNotes:
No oblast-specific facts are documented in the UK Home Office country policy note for Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, and no regional divergence from the national assessment is recorded for this division. Whether enforcement practice in the oblast differs from the national conviction figures is unresolved and not sourced.

The 139 people recorded as impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 are counted nationally; the note does not break that figure down by region, so the oblast's share is unresolved.

The inventory does not establish whether the 101 extremism convictions include any cases originating in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, nor whether local courts have handled administrative and criminal tracks in the same proportions as the national totals.
